content: If a woman declines HIV testing, healthcare providers should address her concerns and, when appropriate, continue to strongly encourage testing. Women who refuse testing because of a prior negative HIV test should be informed about the importance of retesting during each pregnancy. Effective interventions, including antiretroviral therapy and obstetric management, are available to significantly reduce the risk of perinatal HIV transmission. Women at higher risk for HIV, such as those who use illicit drugs, have sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) during pregnancy, have multiple sexual partners during pregnancy, or have HIV-infected partners, should be prioritized for testing. Rapid HIV testing should be performed for women in labor who have undocumented HIV status. If the rapid HIV test result is positive, antiretroviral prophylaxis should be initiated immediately, with the patient’s consent, without waiting for confirmatory test results. All pregnant women should undergo serologic testing for syphilis at their first prenatal visit. In populations with suboptimal prenatal care utilization, rapid plasma reagin (RPR) card test screening and treatment, if reactive, should be performed as soon as pregnancy is confirmed. Women at high risk for syphilis, those living in areas with high syphilis morbidity, those previously untested, or those with positive serology in the first trimester should be screened again early in the third trimester (at 28 weeks of gestation) and at delivery. Some states mandate syphilis screening for all women at delivery. Infants should not be discharged from the hospital unless the mother’s syphilis serologic status has been determined at least once during pregnancy, preferably again at delivery. Any woman delivering a stillborn infant should be tested for syphilis. Pregnant women should be tested for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) during the first trimester of each pregnancy, even if they have been previously vaccinated or tested. Women at high risk for hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, such as those with multiple sexual partners in the past six months, those undergoing evaluation or treatment for an STD, recent or current injection drug users, or those with HBsAg-positive sexual partners, should be retested upon admission to the hospital for delivery. Women at risk for HBV infection should also be vaccinated. To avoid misinterpreting transient positive HBsAg results within 21 days of vaccination, HBsAg testing should be performed before vaccination. Laboratories conducting HBsAg tests must use FDA-cleared assays and follow the manufacturer’s labeling, including confirmatory testing of initially reactive specimens with a licensed neutralizing confirmatory test. When HBsAg testing is performed at the time of delivery admission, shortened testing protocols may be used, and initially reactive results should prompt expedited administration of immunoprophylaxis to infants. All pregnant women should be routinely tested for Chlamydia trachomatis at the first prenatal visit. Women with new or multiple sexual partners should also be retested during the third trimester to prevent maternal postnatal complications and chlamydial infection in the infant. Screening during the first trimester may prevent adverse effects of chlamydia during pregnancy, although evidence supporting this is limited. If screening is only performed during the first trimester, there is a longer period for potential infection acquisition before delivery. Pregnant women at risk for gonorrhea or living in areas with high prevalence of Neisseria gonorrhoeae should be tested at the first prenatal visit. Repeat testing should be performed during the third trimester for those at continued risk. Pregnant women at high risk for hepatitis C infection should be tested for hepatitis C antibodies at the first prenatal visit. High-risk individuals include those with a history of injection drug use, blood transfusion, or organ transplantation before 1992. Routine testing for bacterial vaginosis (BV) is not supported by current evidence. A Papanicolaou (Pap) smear should be obtained at the first prenatal visit if one has not been documented within the preceding year.
